The New Orleans Saints organization mourns the passing of NFL icon Mike Ditka, who passed away today at the age of 86. We extend our deepest condolences to the Ditka family, his loved ones, and the generations of fans who were inspired by his unforgettable presence in our sport.

Mike’s life was defined by an unyielding work ethic, a fierce love for the game, and a relentless determination that helped reshape American football. 

As a pioneer on the field, he revolutionized the tight end position, playing with a signature passion that earned him enshrinement in the Pro Football Hall of Fame before bringing that same legendary competitive fire to the sidelines.

We proudly honor his chapters as a head coach in New Orleans. While his time leading our franchise on the field was brief in longevity, his presence left an indelible mark on our organization. 

Mike approached his tenure with the Saints with the same bold authenticity and relentless drive that defined his entire career. Beyond the wins and losses, his genuine kindness, vibrant personality, and immense generosity to many within our facility created an enduring legacy that our staff and community still fondly remember.

While the football world remembers "Iron Mike" for his unparalleled competitive spirit, we admire the true character, passion, and unique energy he brought to our franchise. His contributions as a player, coach, and lifelong ambassador helped build the modern NFL, and his time in New Orleans will always remain a cherished part of our history.

If you’re surprised Caitlin Clark got snubbed in the WNBA MVP voting on Thursday, then you haven’t been paying attention to the league. Clark put up offensive numbers nobody in the league has ever managed, and yet 19 of the 74 voters decided she wasn’t one of the five best players in the league.

A’ja Wilson charged a fan in the stands, got a technical, and got the MVP. That’s the WNBA. Rudeness gets the trophy. The class act gets left off the ballot.

Wilson won her fifth MVP and took 65 of 74 first-place votes. She led the league at 26.2 points and 1.9 blocks as a center. Her numbers are real. So is her bad behavior.

Wilson got a pass for charging a fan during a game and screaming at him. That in itself tells you all you need to know about the WNBA. On September 29, Game 2 in Indianapolis, a fan pointed and said the foul was on her. Wilson left the play, crossed the baseline, pointed back, and shouted at him. Teammates and security pulled her off it. She got a technical. The fan was walked out, then let back in. No suspension for Wilson.

Clark averaged 22.3 points and 8.3 assists. She’s the first player in league history to finish a season at 20 and 8. She got one first-place vote. She finished fourth, behind Wilson, Olivia Miles, and her own teammate Kelsey Mitchell.

Nineteen of the 74 voters left her off the ballot entirely. She showed up on 55. One first, six seconds, 20 thirds, 16 fourths, 12 fifths, 212 points. Miles had 442. Mitchell had 287.

A voter can put Wilson first based on numbers, but not on behavior. A voter can’t watch Clark achieve the first 20-and-8 season the league has ever had and still leave her off a five-player ballot, like those 19 voters did. That’s not a ranking. That’s leaving Clark out on purpose. Sophie Cunningham said Saturday that something should’ve happened to Wilson when she charged a fan, and that Wilson is the LeBron of the league, so it didn’t. Cunningham was right.

This is why the WNBA doesn’t get respect. It glorifies the player who charges a customer and shrugs at the one who set a record. Wilson got the trophy nine days after the technical. Clark got erased by 19 people with a ballot. The WNBA props up its disgraceful players and ignores its true professionals. That’s why you should ignore the WNBA.
